correctness.rationale: For a blue cell, the white-neighbor count is the sum of the degrees of its row and column in the white-edge graph. Hence the first force requires an isolate and a leaf on opposite sides; edges of any initial cycle can never be the first edge removed from that cycle. At most 2n-2 white edges are possible, and equality forces a single tree plus an isolate. If the isolate is a row, the 2n-2 degree sum on n columns forces a leaf column. Its removal creates a column isolate too, and a forest with isolates on both sides can be eliminated by leaf deletions; transpose for the other type. The bipartite tree formula gives the stated component sizes. A slide is a shared-endpoint white-edge exchange. If it touches the previously isolated row via the added edge, the common endpoint must be a column, so no column degree changes and no cross-type slide can result. For a fixed missing row, insert edges from a chosen active row to each missing adjacent column and drop the last edge of the original tree path to that column; this preserves the tree and shares the column. All other active rows then have degree one and can be pivoted to one column, producing the double star. A center row distinct from two missing rows exists for n>=3, and transferring the leaf edge at the center column connects the two double stars by a slide. A jump can instead delete a leaf column edge and attach the previously missing row to a different column, producing a tree on all rows and all other columns. At n=2 the rook graph is C4: exactly the four adjacent pairs are optimal, a slide produces an opposite pair, and a jump connects the adjacent pairs cyclically. The proof is uniform without enumeration. I inspected the frozen brute force and tree-support programs and recorded checks for n=2,3,4 without executing them; they are corroboration, not an all-size certificate.

evidence: Geneson et al. define adjacency by changing one vertex and prove family results including forests; this is the jump framework and the base rook graph is not a forest. Bong et al. define slides but their forcing predicates are PSD and skew. Benson et al. give product forcing-number results, not minimum-set mobility.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The established frameworks or product theorems do not yield the square-rook ordinary slide components. A jump theorem on a different graph family does not cover this slide-versus-jump comparison.

value.rationale: On a standard graph family, an explicit geometric invariant gives two large connected mobility classes for local moves even though unrestricted moves connect all optima. Legal within-class paths and the exceptional 2-by-2 boundary make this stronger than disconnection alone or a recount of known states.
